common_name: Dare County Yaupon Holly (Virginia Dare Upright Orange-Berried Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; an upright female selection of native yaupon holly named for Virginia Dare and grown for its orange fruit.

directions: Dare County Yaupon Holly is an upright, densely branched female selection discovered in Dare County, North Carolina and named for Virginia Dare, the first English child born in the New World. Unlike the familiar red-berried forms, it sets heavy clusters of bright orange fruit that persist through winter against small, dark evergreen foliage. Its tall, tidy upright habit makes it a strong choice for screens and tall hedges across the Southeast and Gulf Coast. Like other yaupon selections, it tolerates heat, drought, salt spray, and poor soil once established.

common_name: Gray's Greenleaf Yaupon Holly (Glossy Dark-Leaf Heavy-Fruiting Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; a quick-growing female selection of native yaupon holly with glossy dark green foliage and heavy red berry crops.

directions: Gray's Greenleaf Yaupon Holly is a vigorous, quick-growing female selection prized for its unusually glossy, dark green foliage that sets off heavy crops of bright red berries each winter. Its fast fill-in rate and dense branching make it a popular choice for informal hedges and screens where a quicker-establishing native holly is wanted. Like the species, it tolerates heat, drought, and coastal conditions with ease once established, needing only occasional shaping to hold a neat form.

common_name: Otis Miley Yaupon Holly (Small-Leaf Orange-Yellow-Berried Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; a small-leaved female selection of native yaupon holly grown for its orange-yellow fruit.

directions: Otis Miley Yaupon Holly is a female selection distinguished by small leaves and orange-yellow berries, offering an alternative to the more common red-fruited yaupons for winter color variety. It grows with the same dense, twiggy branching typical of native yaupon and works well in mixed screens, hedgerows, or wildlife plantings where birds can feed on the persistent fruit. Once established it tolerates heat, drought, salt spray, and a wide range of soils with minimal care.

common_name: Wiggins Yellow Yaupon Holly (Upright Spreading Yellow-Berried Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; an upright, spreading female selection of native yaupon holly with yellow fruit.

directions: Wiggins Yellow Yaupon Holly, also sold simply as Wiggins, is a female selection with an upright, spreading habit and berries that ripen bright yellow instead of the typical red, adding a different color note to winter plantings. It pairs well with red-berried hollies and other broadleaf evergreens in mixed borders or naturalistic landscapes. As with other yaupon forms, it is tough and adaptable, tolerating heat, drought, salt spray, and poor soil once established.

common_name: Yawkey Yaupon Holly (Rare Amber-Yellow-Berried Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; a rare, open-growing female selection of native yaupon holly grown for its amber-yellow fruit.

directions: Yawkey Yaupon Holly is a scarce female selection valued for its soft amber-yellow berries, a striking departure from the red fruit of typical yaupons, set against small glossy evergreen leaves on an upright, open, spreading frame. Because yaupon is dioecious, it needs a male pollinator, such as the species type or Will Fleming, growing nearby to set its persistent winter fruit. It suits informal screens and specimen plantings better than clipped formal hedges, and shares the species' excellent salt and drought tolerance.

common_name: Dodds Cranberry Yaupon Holly (Upright Crooked-Trunk Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs or small trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; an upright, irregularly branched female selection of native yaupon holly with heavy fruit crops.

directions: Dodds Cranberry Yaupon Holly is a female selection that grows into an upright small tree or large shrub with irregular, somewhat crooked trunks and slender curving branches clothed in small gray-green leaves. Its heavy, showy crops of cranberry-red berries persist through winter and provide food for birds. Given its size it works well as a specimen, screen, or small accent tree, and it tolerates drought, salt spray, and even periodic flooding once established.

common_name: Micron Yaupon Holly (Gremicr Patented Dwarf Fine-Textured Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; patented as Gremicr, a slow-growing, fine-textured dwarf selection of native yaupon holly.

directions: Micron Yaupon Holly, patented as Gremicr under US Plant Patent PP21,168, arose as a naturally occurring branch mutation found on a container-grown yaupon in El Campo, Texas in 1999. It forms an unusually fine-textured, dense, mounding dwarf shrub with leaves smaller than those of Nana or Schillings, and it grows more slowly than either. Its tight, low mounding habit suits foundation plantings, low borders, and small-space landscaping without frequent shearing. Like other dwarf yaupon selections, it tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil with ease.

common_name: Lowrey's Big Leaf Yaupon Holly (Large-Leaf Upright Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; an upright female selection of native yaupon holly with noticeably larger, glossier leaves than the wild species.

directions: Lowrey's Big Leaf Yaupon Holly is an upright female selection notable for glossy leaves distinctly larger than the wild species, giving it a bolder texture in the landscape. It produces bright red berries in fall that persist into winter when a male yaupon pollinator grows nearby. Growing into a substantial large shrub or small tree, it works well as a screen or specimen and fruits most heavily in full sun. It shares the species' strong drought, salt, and soil tolerance.
